screens.title: Behavior Trees for Complex AI
screens.narratorSegment: Today you will learn why Behavior Trees are a practical replacement for sprawling Finite State Machines in medium to large game agents. Rather than managing states and a web of transitions, Behavior Trees let you express behavior as composable tasks and decision nodes that return success, failure, or running. This makes it much easier to add new branches, debug logic, and reuse behaviors across agents. You will see a simple enemy example where the AI prioritizes attack, then chase, then patrol. We will also map the essential node types — Composite, Decorator, and Leaf — to concrete code patterns in Unity. By the end of the lesson you will be able to break a complex goal into sequences and selectors, implement basic Node, Sequence, Selector, Action and Condition classes in C#, and wire them into a top-level tree that ticks each frame. A common misconception is that trees are inherently slower; instead, the tree’s clarity often leads to more predictable evaluation and simpler optimizations. Consider how you would express a reload condition as an early exit in a sequence: that pattern is straightforward in a tree. Hold that idea: behavior expressed as tasks and decisions gives you modular logic that scales.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Behavior Trees
Behavior Trees for Complex AI
Model AI as hierarchical tasks and decisions so you can scale behavior without tangled state transitions.
In this lesson

Contrast FSM limits, learn BT node types, design a simple enemy tree, and implement the basic Node classes in Unity C#.

Why it matters

BTs let you add or tweak behaviors without rewriting a web of transitions. They make debugging and reusing logic across characters easier.

Quick takeaway

Think in tasks: Decompose goals into sequences and selectors before coding behaviors.

Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Root
Ticks into a Selector that chooses an action.
Selector ?
Try attack → chase → patrol until one succeeds.
Sequence →
Check condition THEN perform action; fails fast on condition failure.
FSM limits

State explosion and tangled transitions make maintenance hard.

BT structure

Nodes return Success, Failure, or Running; composites control flow.

Unity implementation

Create Node and derived classes, then tick the root in Update.

screens.title: Why FSMs Break Down
screens.narratorSegment: Finite State Machines are familiar and effective for small, clearly separated behaviors. But as you add behaviors — patrol, chase, attack, flee, reload, call for help — the number of states and transitions grows combinatorially. This is often called state explosion. In a practical game example, adding a single reload action may require linking it from multiple attack states, adding transitions for entering and exiting reload from chase or retreat. That tangled web makes reasoning about what will run under a particular condition difficult. Debugging becomes a navigation task through state graphs instead of focused tasks. A common misconception is that adding more states always clarifies logic; in practice, it often hides it because the behavior is split across many nodes. Instead, think about the desired tasks: check ammo, then shoot; if out of ammo, reload and then resume. This task-oriented view suggests a BT Sequence: condition then action. The clarity you gain means a single reload behavior can be reused instead of duplicated across many states. Reflect on your last AI bug: was it caused by a missing transition? If so, a Behavior Tree might simplify the fix.

keyIdea.title: FSM limitation
keyIdea.text: Adding behaviors creates many states and transitions, which increases maintenance and debugging cost.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › FSM Limits
State explosion explained
A single actor with six behaviors can require many states and transitions, which quickly becomes hard to manage.
Example

An enemy that patrols, chases, attacks, flees, reloads, and calls for help needs many transitions. Adding a reload path often touches several states.

Misconception

More states clarify logic. In reality, splitting a single logical task across states tends to obscure intent and duplicates code.

Key Takeaway

Prefer modular tasks over many specialized states; reuse behavior instead of duplicating transitions.

Analogy

Think of FSMs as many rooms connected by doors. Each new behavior adds doors and rooms until navigation is confusing. A Behavior Tree is like a recipe: steps that read left-to-right and can be reorganized easily.

Try this
List the transitions in an existing FSM and mark where a single action is duplicated. That duplication signals a candidate for a Behavior Tree refactor.

screens.title: What Is a Behavior Tree?
screens.narratorSegment: A Behavior Tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes representing decisions and tasks. At runtime the root is ticked and the tree evaluates nodes top-down. Each node returns one of three values: Success when the task completed, Failure when it could not complete, or Running if the task is underway and should resume on the next tick. This simple contract makes the tree composable: composites inspect child return values and decide which child to run next. Leaf nodes are actions or conditions that touch game state — for example, a condition checks whether the player is within a chase range using distance, and an action moves the agent toward a waypoint. The running state is important: it allows long-running actions like patrol or chase to persist across frames. A pitfall is treating Running as success; it only means the action hasn't finished. Make sure your actions return Success when they complete and Running while in progress. As a quick concrete example, a MoveTo action returns Running while the agent is moving and Success when it reaches the target. Consider how that behavior composes into a Sequence that first checks range, then moves, then attacks.

keyIdea.title: Node contract
keyIdea.text: Nodes must return Success, Failure, or Running so the tree composes predictable behavior across ticks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Behavior Tree Basics
Behavior Tree fundamentals
Nodes evaluate to Success, Failure, or Running. This contract is the foundation of predictable composition.
Root

Entry point that ticks its child. The root initiates evaluation each frame or tick interval.

Composite

Holds multiple children and controls how they are ticked, e.g., Sequence or Selector.

Decorator

Modifies a single child's result or execution, such as inverting success or repeating execution.

Leaf

Action or condition that performs work or checks game state and returns a NodeState.

Concrete example

MoveTo action: while moving it returns Running; when close enough it returns Success. That Running state keeps the agent moving across frames without restarting the action each tick.

Misconception

Treating Running as Success leads to premature branch changes. Running only indicates an incomplete task.

Key Takeaway

Design leaf actions to manage their own progression and return Running until complete.

screens.title: Sequence Node (AND)
screens.narratorSegment: A Sequence node models an AND operation: it executes its children from left to right and only succeeds if all children succeed. If any child returns Failure, the Sequence immediately returns Failure and stops evaluating subsequent children. If a child returns Running, the Sequence returns Running and remembers which child is active so it can resume there on the next tick. This makes Sequence ideal for guarded actions where prerequisites must pass before the main action runs. For example, an Attack sequence might check IsPlayerInAttackRange, then IsWeaponLoaded, then perform Attack. If the weapon is not loaded, the sequence fails immediately and we can hook a higher-level Selector to handle reload or retreat behaviors. A common misconception is to place long-running tasks before quick checks; that pattern hides early exits and causes unnecessary running states. Place cheap conditions first to fail fast. Try building a small sequence in Unity: create condition nodes that test distance and ammo, then an action node that logs Attack. Observe how failure prevents the action from running. Sequence Node (AND) means sequences require all children to succeed and return failure on the first failed child; running pauses progress until resumed.. In practical terms, execute children in order; fail fast on first failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Sequence Node
Sequence: ordered execution
Think "Do A, and then B, and then C." Use when every step must succeed for the whole task to succeed.
Example Sequence
  1. Check: Is player in attack range?
  2. Check: Is weapon loaded?
  3. Action: Perform attack
Pro tip

Place cheap conditions first so the sequence fails fast and avoids running expensive actions unnecessarily.

Supporting bullets
  • Executes children left to right.
  • Returns Failure immediately if any child fails.
  • Returns Running if a child is running and resumes from that child next tick.
  • Succeeds only when all children have succeeded.
Key Takeaway

Use Sequence for guarded tasks where prerequisites must pass before acting.

screens.title: Selector Node (OR)
screens.narratorSegment: A Selector node models an OR operation: it ticks children in order until one returns Success or Running. If a child fails, the Selector proceeds to the next child. The Selector returns Success as soon as a child succeeds, and returns Failure only if every child fails. This makes Selector ideal for priority behavior: try the most desirable option first, then fall back to alternatives. For example, a top-level Selector might try AttackSequence, then ChaseSequence, then Patrol action. If the attack sequence fails because the player is out of range, the Selector moves to chase. If chase is running, the Selector returns Running and resumes the chase on subsequent ticks. A common pitfall is ordering children poorly: if an expensive fallback is placed first, cheaper high-priority options might never be reached. Order children by desirability and cost. Try arranging the enemy tree so attack is first, chase second, and patrol last, then observe debug logs as distance changes. Selector Node (OR) means selectors try children until one succeeds; they are ideal for prioritized fallbacks and choosing the first viable action.. In practical terms, try children until one succeeds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Selector Node
Selector: prioritized choices
Try the best option first; if it fails, try the next. Good for prioritizing attack then chase then patrol.
Example Selector
  1. Attack sequence
  2. Chase sequence
  3. Patrol action
Ordering tip

Place the most desirable, least costly, or most specific options first so they are chosen when applicable.

Supporting bullets
  • Executes children left to right until Success or Running.
  • Returns Failure only if all children fail.
  • Good for fallback logic and prioritization.
Key Takeaway

Order children by desirability so the selector picks the best available action quickly.

screens.title: Decorators: Modifying Child Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Decorator nodes wrap a single child and alter how the child’s result is interpreted or how often it runs. Common decorators include the Inverter, which swaps Success and Failure, and the Repeater, which runs a child multiple times or indefinitely. Decorators help you express meta-behavior without changing the child node itself. For instance, you could place an Inverter on a HasLowHealth condition to create a HasEnoughHealth check, or a Repeater around a Patrol action to make it loop while a condition holds. Decorators are powerful for composing behavior because they keep leaf nodes focused on actions and conditions while providing reusable modifiers for control flow. A frequent misconception is to implement this logic inside action nodes; that duplicates behavior. Instead, use a decorator so the same action can be reused with different modifiers. As a concrete example, wrap a MoveTo action with a Repeater so the agent continues moving between waypoints until an interrupting condition forces the selector to change branches. Decorators: Modifying Child Behavior means decorators change a single child's outcome or repetition behavior without altering the child's implementation.. In practical terms, invert, repeat, or gate a single child's execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Decorator Nodes
Decorators modify a single child
Use them to invert results, repeat execution, or gate a child with a timeout or condition.
Inverter

Flips Success to Failure and Failure to Success. Useful to negate a condition.

Repeater

Runs a child multiple times or indefinitely. Useful to loop patrols or animations.

Design tip

Keep modifiers outside actions so the same action can be reused with different decorators.

Concrete example

Wrap a MoveTo leaf with a Repeater to continuously patrol waypoints. If an Attack sequence succeeds, the selector will choose attack and interrupt the patrol repeater.

Common mistake

Embedding inversion or looping inside actions duplicates code and reduces reusability across the tree.

Key Takeaway

Use decorators to adapt child behavior without changing the child implementation.

screens.title: Action and Condition Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Leaf nodes are where the Behavior Tree connects to the game world. There are two primary kinds: Condition nodes, which check game state and immediately return Success or Failure, and Action nodes, which perform behavior and may return Running while underway. Conditions should be cheap checks like distance tests or ammo counts; actions do movement, animation triggers, or health changes. For example, a Condition node might implement IsPlayerInChaseRange using Vector3 distance; it returns Success if within range and Failure otherwise. An Action node like ChasePlayer will move the transform toward the player and return Running until the agent reaches the player or the condition changes. A common error is to perform expensive calculations in condition nodes or long side effects with conditions; keep conditions focused on observation only. When implementing in Unity, ensure Action nodes perform minimal stateful work and return Success when the action completes, not simply after a single frame. That design preserves predictable composition when these leaves are used inside Sequence and Selector nodes. Action and Condition Nodes means conditions observe state and return success/failure; actions change state and may return running while in progress.. In practical terms, leaf nodes that perform work and check world state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Leaf Nodes
Actions and Conditions
Leaf nodes are the point where the tree inspects or manipulates the game world.
Condition example

IsPlayerInChaseRange uses Vector3 distance and returns Success or Failure immediately.

Action example

ChasePlayer moves the agent toward the player and returns Running until arrival, then Success.

Best practice

Keep conditions cheap and side-effect free. Actions should manage progression and report Running until done.

Common mistake

Putting heavy logic inside condition nodes or returning Success prematurely from actions breaks composition and makes debugging harder.

Concrete check

Distance check example: compare Vector3.Distance to chaseRange to return Success for conditions used in sequences.

Try this

Implement a simple IsPlayerInAttackRange condition and an Attack action that logs messages; observe how the sequence behaves when the condition fails.

Key Takeaway

Design leaves to be small, focused, and reusable across composite nodes.

screens.title: Ticking and NodeState Flow
screens.narratorSegment: The Behavior Tree is evaluated by ticking the root node at a regular interval, typically once per Update frame. The root calls Evaluate on its children according to the composite logic. When a child returns Running, the composite marks that child so the next tick resumes from the same point. This memory is crucial for actions like chasing or patrolling that span many frames. For example, when a Chase sequence hits a Running state during MoveTo, the sequence returns Running and on the next tick will re-evaluate the same MoveTo leaf instead of restarting earlier checks. Composites such as Sequence and Selector have different handling for Running: Sequence may record the index of the running child to resume, while Selector treats a running child as running for the entire selector and returns Running immediately. A common misunderstanding is assuming a tick always restarts evaluation from the first child; it does restart from the root but well-designed nodes remember progress by returning Running rather than Success. In Unity implement this by storing minimal state in nodes (like current child index) so resumes are efficient. Test this by making Chase return Running and observing that the distance check does not repeatedly re-trigger unreachable code.

narration.text: The Behavior Tree is evaluated by ticking the root node at a regular interval, typically once per Update frame. The root calls Evaluate on its children according to the composite logic. When a child returns Running, the composite marks that child so the next tick resumes from the same point. This memory is crucial for actions like chasing or patrolling that span many frames. For example, when a Chase sequence hits a Running state during MoveTo, the sequence returns Running and on the next tick will re-evaluate the same MoveTo leaf instead of restarting earlier checks. Composites such as Sequence and Selector have different handling for Running: Sequence may record the index of the running child to resume, while Selector treats a running child as running for the entire selector and returns Running immediately. A common misunderstanding is assuming a tick always restarts evaluation from the first child; it does restart from the root but well-designed nodes remember progress by returning Running rather than Success. In Unity implement this by storing minimal state in nodes (like current child index) so resumes are efficient. Test this by making Chase return Running and observing that the distance check does not repeatedly re-trigger unreachable code.

Call Evaluate on the root each frame. Nodes use the Running state to maintain progress between ticks.
Resume behavior

If a child returns Running, composites should resume from that child on the next Evaluate rather than restarting earlier children unnecessarily.

screens.title: Designing an Enemy Behavior Tree
screens.narratorSegment: Design starts with the agent's goals and failure cases. For a basic enemy the primary goals might be to attack when in range, chase when the player is nearby but not close enough, and patrol otherwise. Translate that into a top-level Selector that tries an Attack sequence, then a Chase sequence, then a Patrol action as a fallback. Each Attack or Chase sequence is composed of a condition check followed by an action: for Attack, check attack range then attack; for Chase, check chase range then chase. This hierarchical design keeps concerns isolated: Range checks are conditions and movement or combat are actions. The design also makes it easy to add more branches like a Flee sequence when health is low or a CallForHelp action without changing existing nodes. A design pitfall is duplicating checks across branches; instead encapsulate reusable checks and actions as leaf nodes and reference them in multiple composites. Before coding, sketch the tree and annotate which leaves return Running, Success, or Failure so you can reason about ticking behavior in play mode. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Code Walkthrough
Node and composite patterns
Implement NodeState enum and an abstract Node with Evaluate. Sequence and Selector iterate children and update nodeState accordingly.
// NodeState { Running, Success, Failure }
public abstract class Node { protected NodeState nodeState; public abstract NodeState Evaluate(); }

public class Sequence : Node {
  private List children;
  public Sequence(List children){ this.children = children; }
  public override NodeState Evaluate(){ bool anyRunning=false; foreach(var node in children){ switch(node.Evaluate()){ case NodeState.Running: anyRunning=true; break; case NodeState.Success: continue; case NodeState.Failure: nodeState=NodeState.Failure; return nodeState; } } nodeState = anyRunning? NodeState.Running : NodeState.Success; return nodeState; }
}

public class Selector : Node { /* similar pattern: return Success on first Success */ }
Supporting bullets
  • Keep Evaluate side-effect free except at leaf nodes.
  • Store minimal state in composites to resume Running children.
  • Use Debug.Log in leaves to trace behavior flow during play.
Common mistake

Not setting nodeState before return. Always set nodeState so debugging output matches runtime behavior.

Key Takeaway

Follow the Evaluate contract strictly and log leaf execution to verify flow in Unity.

fullNarratorScript:
Today you will learn why Behavior Trees are a practical replacement for sprawling Finite State Machines in medium to large game agents. Rather than managing states and a web of transitions, Behavior Trees let you express behavior as composable tasks and decision nodes that return success, failure, or running. This makes it much easier to add new branches, debug logic, and reuse behaviors across agents. You will see a simple enemy example where the AI prioritizes attack, then chase, then patrol. We will also map the essential node types — Composite, Decorator, and Leaf — to concrete code patterns in Unity. By the end of the lesson you will be able to break a complex goal into sequences and selectors, implement basic Node, Sequence, Selector, Action and Condition classes in C#, and wire them into a top-level tree that ticks each frame. A common misconception is that trees are inherently slower; instead, the tree’s clarity often leads to more predictable evaluation and simpler optimizations. Consider how you would express a reload condition as an early exit in a sequence: that pattern is straightforward in a tree. Hold that idea: behavior expressed as tasks and decisions gives you modular logic that scales.

Over these screens you'll gain clear, assessable skills. First, you will identify why Finite State Machines become hard to manage as behaviors multiply, recognizing the state explosion and tangled transition problem with a concrete enemy that patrols, chases, attacks, and flees. Second, you will understand the core structure of a Behavior Tree: root, composite, decorator, and leaf nodes, and how these return success, failure, or running. Third, you will differentiate composite types — Sequence and Selector — and know when to apply each one in practice, such as guarding an attack with a sequence of checks. Fourth, you will sketch and test a simple Behavior Tree for an enemy that prioritizes attack, then chase, then patrol, turning design into a small playable experiment. Each objective links to a small competency milestone so you can verify understanding. As you progress, try to map each objective to a small coding task: reproduce the enemy tree, run it in play mode, and verify debug messages. That hands-on verification is how you move from knowing to doing.

These next objectives focus on turning a design into working Unity code and testing it in play mode. You will implement a basic Behavior Tree system in C# by creating a base Node class and deriving Sequence, Selector, Action, and Condition nodes. You will learn the NodeState pattern: methods return Success, Failure, or Running so the tree can remember progress across ticks. You will construct an EnemyBehaviorTree that sets up leaf actions like Chase and Attack and conditions that measure distance to the player. Finally, you will test and iterate: tick the root in Update or at a fixed interval, observe debug messages, and adjust ranges and ordering until the behavior matches design. Each skill includes a small verification step so you can confirm correctness. This hands-on focus ensures you not only know the theory but can maintain and evolve AI systems in an actual Unity project.

Finite State Machines are familiar and effective for small, clearly separated behaviors. But as you add behaviors — patrol, chase, attack, flee, reload, call for help — the number of states and transitions grows combinatorially. This is often called state explosion. In a practical game example, adding a single reload action may require linking it from multiple attack states, adding transitions for entering and exiting reload from chase or retreat. That tangled web makes reasoning about what will run under a particular condition difficult. Debugging becomes a navigation task through state graphs instead of focused tasks. A common misconception is that adding more states always clarifies logic; in practice, it often hides it because the behavior is split across many nodes. Instead, think about the desired tasks: check ammo, then shoot; if out of ammo, reload and then resume. This task-oriented view suggests a BT Sequence: condition then action. The clarity you gain means a single reload behavior can be reused instead of duplicated across many states. Reflect on your last AI bug: was it caused by a missing transition? If so, a Behavior Tree might simplify the fix.

A Behavior Tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes representing decisions and tasks. At runtime the root is ticked and the tree evaluates nodes top-down. Each node returns one of three values: Success when the task completed, Failure when it could not complete, or Running if the task is underway and should resume on the next tick. This simple contract makes the tree composable: composites inspect child return values and decide which child to run next. Leaf nodes are actions or conditions that touch game state — for example, a condition checks whether the player is within a chase range using distance, and an action moves the agent toward a waypoint. The running state is important: it allows long-running actions like patrol or chase to persist across frames. A pitfall is treating Running as success; it only means the action hasn't finished. Make sure your actions return Success when they complete and Running while in progress. As a quick concrete example, a MoveTo action returns Running while the agent is moving and Success when it reaches the target. Consider how that behavior composes into a Sequence that first checks range, then moves, then attacks.

A Sequence node models an AND operation: it executes its children from left to right and only succeeds if all children succeed. If any child returns Failure, the Sequence immediately returns Failure and stops evaluating subsequent children. If a child returns Running, the Sequence returns Running and remembers which child is active so it can resume there on the next tick. This makes Sequence ideal for guarded actions where prerequisites must pass before the main action runs. For example, an Attack sequence might check IsPlayerInAttackRange, then IsWeaponLoaded, then perform Attack. If the weapon is not loaded, the sequence fails immediately and we can hook a higher-level Selector to handle reload or retreat behaviors. A common misconception is to place long-running tasks before quick checks; that pattern hides early exits and causes unnecessary running states. Place cheap conditions first to fail fast. Try building a small sequence in Unity: create condition nodes that test distance and ammo, then an action node that logs Attack. Observe how failure prevents the action from running. Sequence Node (AND) means sequences require all children to succeed and return failure on the first failed child; running pauses progress until resumed.. In practical terms, execute children in order; fail fast on first failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Selector node models an OR operation: it ticks children in order until one returns Success or Running. If a child fails, the Selector proceeds to the next child. The Selector returns Success as soon as a child succeeds, and returns Failure only if every child fails. This makes Selector ideal for priority behavior: try the most desirable option first, then fall back to alternatives. For example, a top-level Selector might try AttackSequence, then ChaseSequence, then Patrol action. If the attack sequence fails because the player is out of range, the Selector moves to chase. If chase is running, the Selector returns Running and resumes the chase on subsequent ticks. A common pitfall is ordering children poorly: if an expensive fallback is placed first, cheaper high-priority options might never be reached. Order children by desirability and cost. Try arranging the enemy tree so attack is first, chase second, and patrol last, then observe debug logs as distance changes. Selector Node (OR) means selectors try children until one succeeds; they are ideal for prioritized fallbacks and choosing the first viable action.. In practical terms, try children until one succeeds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Decorator nodes wrap a single child and alter how the child’s result is interpreted or how often it runs. Common decorators include the Inverter, which swaps Success and Failure, and the Repeater, which runs a child multiple times or indefinitely. Decorators help you express meta-behavior without changing the child node itself. For instance, you could place an Inverter on a HasLowHealth condition to create a HasEnoughHealth check, or a Repeater around a Patrol action to make it loop while a condition holds. Decorators are powerful for composing behavior because they keep leaf nodes focused on actions and conditions while providing reusable modifiers for control flow. A frequent misconception is to implement this logic inside action nodes; that duplicates behavior. Instead, use a decorator so the same action can be reused with different modifiers. As a concrete example, wrap a MoveTo action with a Repeater so the agent continues moving between waypoints until an interrupting condition forces the selector to change branches. In practical terms, invert, repeat, or gate a single child's execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Leaf nodes are where the Behavior Tree connects to the game world. There are two primary kinds: Condition nodes, which check game state and immediately return Success or Failure, and Action nodes, which perform behavior and may return Running while underway. Conditions should be cheap checks like distance tests or ammo counts; actions do movement, animation triggers, or health changes. For example, a Condition node might implement IsPlayerInChaseRange using Vector3 distance; it returns Success if within range and Failure otherwise. An Action node like ChasePlayer will move the transform toward the player and return Running until the agent reaches the player or the condition changes. A common error is to perform expensive calculations in condition nodes or long side effects with conditions; keep conditions focused on observation only. When implementing in Unity, ensure Action nodes perform minimal stateful work and return Success when the action completes, not simply after a single frame. That design preserves predictable composition when these leaves are used inside Sequence and Selector nodes.
